Oil & gas · Tanzania

Pipeline wayleave mapping in Tanzania

Tanzania’s pipelines are long and mostly rural, yet towns and villages grow towards them. The Petroleum Act requires a licensee to acquire wayleaves around its petroleum installations and says owners on or bordering a wayleave must not interfere with the licensee’s rights (s.186). We give your land, integrity and environmental and social teams a dated inventory of what stands inside each band of the wayleave, and what changed since the last survey.

Send your route for a proposal See sample outputs

The problem, in your words

Inside the wayleave, between patrols

A pipeline wayleave in Tanzania can cross hundreds of kilometres of village land, farmland and bush, and pass the edge of towns that did not exist when it was laid. What appears on it becomes somebody’s problem: a safety hazard, a future compensation cost, or a dispute about who was there first.

“There are new structures inside the wayleave.”

Houses, shops, workshops and fences can go up on and beside the right of way, especially where a line passes a trading centre or runs near a road. A structure is easier to discuss with the village council and the owner while it is new and alone.

“Someone has been digging near the line.”

Works near a buried line show at the surface first: fresh digging, spoil, trenches, footpaths and tracks that were not there before. Altering, removing or connecting to a pipeline without the licensee’s consent is an offence under the Petroleum Act, s.240, and under s.240(4) an offence of economic and organised crime.

“The line is built. What is our baseline?”

Once the pipe is buried and the right of way reinstated, the land team needs a dated picture of what stands in and around it on day one of operation, to measure everything after against.

“Our lenders want dated evidence.”

Environmental and social monitoring on a lender-financed line asks what has changed around the right of way since the cut-off date, and where. Site visits are periodic; dated imagery fills the gaps between them.

Who this is for

  • Pipeline land and wayleave officers
  • Integrity and asset teams, as users of structure data
  • Environmental and social managers
  • Community-relations and grievance teams
  • Lenders’ environmental and social monitors
  • Operations and maintenance contractors
  • ESIA, RAP and valuation consultancies
  • GIS and asset-records teams

The law in Tanzania

What the register is measured against

A summary of the public rules as of 27 September 2026, for orientation. It is not legal advice; the full explanation, with sources, is in our wayleave-law guide.

Instrument What it sets for pipelines
Petroleum Act, Cap. 392, s.185 A licensee takes “all necessary measures to secure acquisition of rights of way for laying, operation and repair of gas pipelines”, subject to the Gas Utilisation Master Plan and in consultation with EWURA
Petroleum Act, s.186 The licensee acquires “wayleave around existing and future gas infrastructure and petroleum installations”; owners on or bordering a wayleave “shall not interfere with a licensee’s acquired rights”; compensation disputes go under the Land Acquisition Act
Petroleum Act, s.240 Offences for altering, removing or connecting to “any pipeline or gas installations without consent of the licensee”, including attempts and assistance
Land Act, Cap. 113, ss.161, 166, 186–187 A wayleave runs with the land and binds every occupier; compensation for trees, crops and buildings; the Commissioner’s removal orders for obstructions and encroachments on a public right of way, and the offence of not complying
Tanzania-Zambia Pipeline Act, Cap. 40, s.5 The statute behind one cross-border products pipeline; we found no strip width in it

Safety zones are upstream. The Petroleum Act’s s.203 safety zones, whose extent PURA determines, sit in the Part on upstream operations. They surround wells and upstream processing, not crude or products pipelines and their pump stations. For gas fields, gas transmission lines and the LNG site, see gas pipelines and LNG in Tanzania.

We found no single statutory width for a pipeline wayleave, so we report the bands you set from your own acquisition, agreement or company standard. In Swahili documents a crude-oil pipeline is bomba la mafuta ghafi. Wayleave law in Tanzania

What we map along the line

A register of what stands in the wayleave, then what changed

We buffer the route you supply in its UTM zone, list each structure the review confirms with its distance to the line and its band, and cut the route into 500 m stretches. Each stretch is rated for encroachment density: high where more than five structures stand inside the widest band, medium for one to five, low for none. It is a count rule that tells your wayleave officers where to go first, not a safety or integrity rating.

After the baseline, the route is re-surveyed on a schedule you agree with us. New and removed structures between dated surveys are flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, with before-and-after views, and your team receives a notice after each survey saying what changed and where. Fresh digging, spoil, trenches and new tracks across the line are flagged the same way, so patrols know where to look. They do not replace patrols.

Every report names the imagery and its capture date, so the register can be read against a valuation date, a cut-off date or the day the line entered operation.

What you receive

  • A structure register: ID, distance to the line, band, chainage and coordinates
  • An encroachment-density rating for each 500 m stretch
  • New and removed structures between surveys, with before-and-after views
  • A change notice after each survey
  • Fresh excavation, spoil and new tracks near the line, flagged for checking
  • Settlement growth trends around the line
  • A PDF report in English, with GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers

Reading a register

This is a stretch rated high in our pipeline sample: sixteen structures within 100 m of one 500 m stretch, each listed with its distance and band. The sample uses the same register format and rating rule as a delivered survey; its marks were placed by a reviewer on a basemap shown for illustration. On a Tanzanian line the same view is measured to the bands of your wayleave, and the report names the imagery used and its capture date.

From construction to operation

A dated record for the life of the line

A cross-border crude pipeline, most of its length in Tanzania, is nearing completion and moving from construction into operation. When a line goes into service, the land questions change. The construction corridor is reinstated, and the next questions are about what is built near the pipe, where new tracks cross it and where ground is dug.

A baseline survey soon after reinstatement records the structures, tracks and cleared ground in the right of way and the bands around it, stretch by stretch. Scheduled re-surveys then show what is new, what has gone and where settlement is growing towards the line. The record sits next to the operator’s own patrols, control-room monitoring and community monitoring programmes; it does not replace them.

Where the register fits

  • A dated land-use record for the right of way and its surroundings
  • A ranked list of stretches for patrol and wayleave teams to visit
  • Change between survey dates, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Location checks for grievances against the imagery history
  • Leak, tap, theft or integrity detection
  • Alerts between surveys
  • Anything about people

Environmental and social compliance

Dated evidence for lenders’ monitoring

Lender-financed pipelines report against the IFC Performance Standards and, for banks that have adopted them, the Equator Principles. Performance Standard 5 asks for a census and a cut-off date for eligibility that is “well documented and disseminated”, and it has no duty to compensate those who encroach on the project area after a cut-off date that was clearly established and made public (paras 12 and 23). Tanzanian law points the same way: the High Court has held that developments made after the valuation and notice are not compensable.

Between site visits, a dated register answers the monitoring questions directly: how many structures stand in and around the right of way on each survey date, which are new since the cut-off date, and where resettlement sites and host villages are growing. For a single grievance point, a location check sets every dated image covering it side by side, so the grievance team can see what was there on each date.

Supports, never replaces

  • The census, the asset inventory and the valuation stay with the valuers and the RAP team
  • The register describes what the imagery shows, not who lives there
  • Eligibility and compensation are decided under Tanzanian law and the project’s resettlement framework

Valuation and cut-off baselines in Tanzania

New lines

Route options and a baseline before the valuation

New cross-border refined-products pipelines are being planned in Tanzania, and a products pipeline built in the 1960s now runs through towns that have grown up around it. A new line starts with route options. We count the structures along each alternative alignment within the same bands, so route engineers and the land team can compare options on the land they would affect, alongside their engineering and environmental criteria. Slope, drainage crossings and ground that has flooded in past satellite records are screened along each option.

Once the route is chosen, a dated baseline records the corridor before the valuation, and a second on the cut-off date shows what appeared in between. The comparison is one input to route selection, not a full alternatives assessment.

Village land along the route

Where a route crosses village land, the transfer runs under the Village Land Act, s.4: a gazetted notice at least 90 days ahead, the village council informing the villagers affected, the village assembly’s approval for land under 250 ha, and no transfer until compensation is agreed or the High Court approves an interim payment (s.4(8)). A structure baseline before the notice, and another when compensation is agreed, give the valuers two fixed points. See wayleave law in Tanzania.

Drone checks near pipelines

Where a drone helps, and what it needs first

Satellite screening narrows the search; a drone survey of the flagged stretches then captures the detail your team needs, subject to the TCAA approvals and security clearances each job requires. Under the Civil Aviation (Remotely Piloted Aircraft Systems) Regulations, 2026, that means an operator with a Tanzanian principal place of business and an RPAS Operator Certificate, a security clearance, registered drones, vetted pilots and TCAA’s authorisation for each operation, with a risk assessment submitted at least 14 days ahead.

A wayleave lined with homes is the hard case: flights keep 50 m from people and structures not under the operator’s control unless TCAA approves otherwise. Afridrone is working towards Tanzanian drone approvals, and every drone proposal names the company that will fly and the approvals its flights need.

Near pump stations and terminals

Plan any flight near a pump station, block valve or terminal with the operator’s written permission and through its site security, and with the consents GN 268 requires for launch and recovery (reg 86). Protected places stay out of every deliverable.

Drone law in Tanzania

Local content

What the Petroleum Act means for this service

Licence holders, contractors and subcontractors in Tanzania’s petroleum sector “shall give preference to goods which are produced or available in Tanzania and services which are rendered by Tanzanian citizens or local companies” (Petroleum Act, s.219(1)). Goods and services not available locally are supplied by a company in a joint venture with a local company that owns at least 25 per cent of it, or as the regulations provide (s.219(2)–(3)). A “local company” is incorporated under the Companies Act and wholly owned by Tanzanian citizens, or is in a joint venture or partnership with Tanzanian citizens holding at least 15 per cent (s.219(9)). Each AfriScan proposal for petroleum work states which company contracts and how the proposal meets s.219; the notes for working with us in Tanzania set out the rest.

How it works

From route file to reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the route or the wayleave polygon, the regions it crosses, the widths that matter and what the record is for: operations, lenders’ monitoring, a valuation or a new route. We agree the bands, the imagery and the deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Screen from satellite

    Structures and ground change are mapped along the whole route from dated satellite imagery, open building datasets or the imagery you hold. No one goes to site.

  3. Check up close

    Drone surveys capture the stretches that need detail, subject to the TCAA approvals and security clearances each job requires.

  4. Review and deliver

    A person checks every result; each structure is measured, banded and rated, and the report goes to the contacts you name with the GIS layers.

What this survey is, and what it is not

Onshore only. It maps structures, cleared ground, tracks and excavations visible from above, reviewed by a person. It does not detect leaks, taps, theft or pipe condition, it cannot see through optical cloud, it is not a cadastral survey, and it complements your own line monitoring rather than replacing it. See the global oil and gas page and our methodology.

Frequently asked questions

Does this replace our patrols and line monitoring?

No. Pipeline operators run their own patrols, control-room monitoring and community programmes, and some lay fibre-optic cable along the line for monitoring. The register adds something those systems are not built to give, a dated, reviewed record of the structures, cleared ground, tracks and excavations in and around the right of way, so patrol, land and community teams know where the ground has changed. Patrols, response and security stay with your own teams.

Can you detect leaks, illegal taps or theft?

No. Imagery cannot see a tap, a leak or the condition of the pipe. We flag what is visible at the surface, such as fresh digging, spoil, new tracks and footpaths across the line, cleared ground and new structures, so your field teams know where to check.

Which widths do you measure against?

The wayleave width in your own acquisition or agreement, and the bands you choose inside and around it, for example 0–15 m, 15–30 m and 30–60 m from the centreline, up to six in one survey. We found no single statutory width for a pipeline wayleave in Tanzanian law, so the widths come from you. If you send the wayleave as a polygon, we report what stands inside it as well.

Can the register support our lenders' environmental and social reporting?

Yes, as a dated input. On a pipeline financed under the IFC Performance Standards or the Equator Principles, the register records the structures in and around the right of way on each survey date, what is new since the cut-off date, and where a grievance point sits against the imagery history. It supports your census, resettlement and livelihood monitoring; it does not replace them or decide eligibility.

Will you publish maps of our line?

No. Results go only to the contacts you name. We never publish maps of your line, its stations or the settlements around it without your written permission, and protected places are left out of every deliverable.

How does the weather affect the survey?

Optical satellite imagery needs clear skies, so we plan captures for clearer spells and work from the best recent archive scenes, and each report states the imagery dates. Radar satellite comparisons can show larger changes, such as clearing, earthworks and new large buildings, even under rainy-season cloud; those flags are followed up with optical imagery or a drone check.

Send us your route file

KML, KMZ, GeoJSON, Shapefile, GPX or GeoPackage, or the wayleave as a polygon. Tell us the product (crude oil or refined products), the regions the line crosses, the widths in your wayleave and what the record is for: operations, lenders' monitoring, a valuation or a new route. We reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
